column1: Case Report Zimmermann–Laband syndromeassociated hereditary gingival fibromatosis Jaishree Tukaram Kshirsagar, Kalaiselvan Dharani, Priyangha Thangavel Abstract: Hereditary gingival fibromatosis (HGF) is an uncommon slow‑growing fibrous overgrowth characterized by connective tissue accumulation.   It presents as an isolated feature or as a manifestation of any syndrome.

Various syndromes associated with HGF are inherited by autosomal dominant/recessive/X‑linked traits.   Zimmermann–Laband syndrome (ZLS) is a rare, autosomal dominant inherited disease manifested with gingival fibromatosis (GF), nose and ears abnormalities, and hypoplastic/dysplastic nails or terminal phalanges of hand and feet. Although the pattern of inheritance was found to be both autosomal dominant and recessive traits, the molecular basis is still unclear.

This report presents a possible case of ZLS‑associated HGF in a 25‑year‑old female patient who presents with GF, hypertrichosis, and other syndrome‑related features. Her father was similarly affected whereas her mother and sibling were asymptomatic. The patient and her family members were explained about the condition and surgical periodontal therapy was carried out for the patient to improve esthetics and was followed up regularly.

Esthetics was significantly improved, and no recurrence was noted at the end of 6 months. Key words: Gingival enlargement, hereditary gingival fibromatosis, syndromic gingival fibromatosis, Zimmermann–Laband syndrome INTRODUCTION Hereditary gingival fibromatosis (HGF) is an uncommon gingival disease of genetic origin. It is a fibrous overgrowth that is benign in nature, grows slowly, and is characterized mainly by the accumulation of connective tissue fibroblasts.

It presents either as an isolated feature or as a manifestation of any syndrome, covering the tooth to varying extents. The 2017 classification of periodontal and peri‑implant diseases and condition categorized gingival fibromatosis (GF) under nonbiofilm induced gingival diseases.   Nonsyndromic (isolated) HGF may be inherited by autosomal dominant trait whereas the syndromic form is characterized by autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive or even Xlinked inheritance.

Various syndromes associated with HGF are GF with hypertrichosis, Zimmermann–Laband syndrome (ZLS), Ramon syndrome, Murray–Puretic–Drescher syndrome, Rutherford syndrome, Cross syndrome, Prune belly syndrome, Cantu syndrome, etc., ZLS is a rare heterogeneous congenital disorder affecting the facial areas and the extremities.   Local or diffuse, nonhemorrhagic GF is the predominant manifestation followed by long and thin fingers and toes with hypoplastic or aplastic nails at birth.   The secondary features are skeletal deformities of the maxillary arch, i.e., open bite, protruding jaws, macroglossia, higharched palate, multiple unerupted teeth, abnormalities of soft cartilages of nose and ears, strabismus, hypertrichosis, intellectual deficiency, hepatosplenomegaly, hyperextensibility of joints, and mild hirsutism.

The pattern of inheritance was found in both autosomal dominant and recessive traits, but the molecular basis is still unclear.   This case report presents a possible case of ZLS and its periodontal management. CASE REPORT A 25year-old female patient reported with the chief complaint of enlarged gums of several years duration.

Gingivectomy was planned to improve esthetics.   External bevel gingivectomy with a surgical guide was done under local anesthesia at 2 weeks’ interval in the areas with GF.   The periodontal dressing was placed and 0.12% chlorhexidine mouth rinse was advised for 2 weeks, postsurgically [Figure 6].

The excised gingival tissues were sent for histopathological examination.   Histopathology revealed the presence of hyperplastic parakeratinized squamous epithelium of variable thickness and bundles of dense collagenous fibrous connective tissue exhibiting hyalinization of collagen with focal areas of inflammatory cells  [Figure 7].

Esthetics in terms of gingival appearance improved significantly, and no recurrence was noted at the end of the 6th month, postoperatively [Figure 8]. DISCUSSION GF is a slow‑growing fibrous overgrowth of gingival connective tissue, caused by various factors such as drugs, hormonal changes, and genetics.

It can also present as a manifestation of systemic diseases such as leukemia, lymphoma, Wegener’s granulomatosis, sarcoidosis, and oral granulomatosis.   The genetically induced GF is of two forms – syndromic and nonsyndromic.   Nonsyndromic HGF might be inherited by a singlegene mutation whereas multiple gene mutations or gene dosage effect might result in syndromic HGF.

The first case of HGF reported by William H Goddard was found to be nonsyndromic with the autosomal dominant trait, where the mutation was noted in son of sevenless1 gene in locus 2p21p22.   Chromosomes 2p13p16, 4q21, and 5q1322 are also genetically linked to the autosomal dominant trait of HGF.   The inheritance pattern of syndromic HGF might be autosomal dominant or recessive or even Xlinked trait.

In the present case report, a 25year-old female patient was diagnosed as a possible case of ZLS based on the familial history, clinical features, and hematological, biochemical, and histopathological investigations. ZLS is a rare autosomal dominant congenital disorder affecting facial areas and extremities.

The mutation in the CACNA2D3 gene, LRTM1gene, WTN5A gene, and ERC2 gene located in chromosome 3p14.3 is responsible for ZLS. Stefanova et al. have assessed the 3p breakpoint location and have found mutation in CACNA2D3 gene and WTN5A gene in a mother and daughter with ZLS.   Hoogendijk et al. have documented a chromosomal insertion in chromosome 8 (12;8)

(p11.2; - q11.2q24.3) in a patient with ZLS and stated that mutation in chromosome 8 is the prime etiology for the syndrome. Shirian et al. have detected mutations at 3q13.13, 1q25.2, 1p12, and also in 19q12 in a patient with typical clinical features of ZLS.   Guglielmi et al.  Have identified mutation in KCNH1 gene and Galal et al.  Have detected mutation in ATP6V1B2 gene, respectively.

Even though various studies have reported different inheritance patterns for ZLS, the molecular basis is still not clear. The clinical presentation of HGF may vary, exhibiting minimal involvement characterized by enlargement of maxillary tuberosity and mandibular molar gingiva, to severe involvement encompassing both maxillary and mandibular gingiva covering the crowns of the teeth completely.   In the present case report, the involvement was said to be moderate as the GF has involved maxillary gingiva alone covering 2/3rd the crowns of the teeth.

However, the patient was presented with the manifestations of ZLS without phalangeal involvement.   Castori et al.  Have reported that gingival hypertrophy with and without phalangeal involvement has been considered explicit characteristic of ZLS. Shah and Gupta have reported a case of a 3.5year-old child with ZLS associated with bilateral cataract.

Lin et al. documented a case of ZLS with thymic hyperplasia, ventricular hypertrophy, and aortic dilation.   Since the patient reported after puberty, thymic hyperplasia was not evaluated directly as thymus undergoes genetic involution at puberty. However, thymic hyperplasia is usually associated with myasthenia gravis and hyperthyroidism in most of the cases.

Hence, symptoms of myasthenia gravis such as shortness of breath, difficulty in swallowing, blurred or double vision, weakness of eye muscles, impaired speech, and ptosis of the eyelid were evaluated. No significant symptoms were noted and hence ruled out.   To rule out hyperthyroidism, thyroid function tests were performed.

Thyroid levels were normal and hence, ruled out.   Ventricular hypertrophy and aortic dilation were ruled out as no significant clinical symptoms such as chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath and heart murmurs were noted.   Since clinical interpretations were negative, no radiographic or advanced imaging interventions were carried out further.

The histologic appearance of HGF is usually characterized by parakeratinized, squamous hyperplastic epithelium with elongated rete pegs and a fibrous, acellular connective tissue with fibroblast cells.   Calcified particles, amyloid deposits, and odontogenic epithelial islands are unusual findings. The genetic mutation increases the production of β1 transforming growth factor (TGFβ1), which enhances the transdifferentiation of gingival myofibroblasts resulting in GF.

There are histopathological and cell culture reports in the literature which documented the presence of myofibroblasts.   The recent research stated that the interferonγ could attenuate the transdifferentiated myofibroblast‑induced extracellular matrix accumulation and thus, might be helpful in the prevention of HGF. Guglielmi et al. have documented an increased inflammatory state proteinsdefensins alpha 1 and 3 in salivary proteome of a 3year-old child with ZLS compared to healthy subjects of the same sex and age and also noted the presence of S100A7.

Thus, proteomic analysis serves as an adjunctive method of diagnosis of rare diseases with differentially expressed proteins and peptides. The periodontal management can be done surgically to improve the esthetics by restoring the gingival contours.   The surgical management includes external or internal bevel gingivectomy, and apically displaced flap which can be done with a scalpel or cryosurgery and laser, but the predictability of longterm results is still unclear.

It has been documented in various literature that the plaque accumulation mediates the recurrence rate of fibromatosis as the recurrence is higher in areas with severe plaque accumulation and minimal or delayed in patients with good oral hygiene. Hence, the treated patients should be recalled and reviewed at regular intervals.   Professional cleaning and oral hygiene instructions should be reinforced to reduce the recurrence rate.

In this case report, quadrantwise external bevel gingivectomy was done at regular intervals, and the patient was followed up periodically.   A significant improvement in the esthetics and no recurrence was noted at the end of 6 months. Hence, a multidisciplinary approach, involving geneticist, periodontist, pathologist, biochemist, and psychologist, is required for proper diagnosis and appropriate treatment of the disease.

More studies should be focused on proteomics to identify molecular markers for early diagnosis and correlation of dental and genetic phenotypes.   TGFβ1 has found to be primarily associated with GF, but evidence supporting counteraction of TGFβ1 are still lacking and needs to be explored.   Thus, future studies investigating the suppressing action of interferon against TGFβ1 should be evolved to prevent the development of HGF.
